newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds underperform as US Fed rattles markets.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds underperform as US Fed rattles markets.

text.p: Irish bonds underperformed on Tuesday as bond markets across the globe were shaken by warnings of latent U.S. inflation from Federal Reserve governor Alan Greenspan.

Dealers said the five-year spread of Irish bonds over German Bunds widened by 10 basis points before clawing back a little, while the 10-year spread stretched out about seven basis points. The 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was yielding 5.81 percent late on Tuesday, down from 5.68 at Monday's close. The benchmark 8.0 percent stock due 2006 saw its yield rise to 6.55 percent from 6.40.

"We were awaiting Greenspan's testimony for most of the day and have lost ground to Bunds," one dealer said. "The short end has been hit hardest." In testimony to the U.S. Senate Budget Committee, Greenspan warned of the risks of wage-driven inflation as a prolonged period of perceived job insecurity came to an end.
U.S. Treasuries were panicked and headed firmly south although they later clambered back into positive ground.
No such luck for the Irish bond market, with the 10-year benchmark trading at 110.10 by 1600 GMT, well below Monday's close of 110.35.
Greenspan's testimony forced bond dealers to put speculation about Wednesday's Irish budget on the backburner.
Irish finance minister Ruairi Quinn will unveil his 1997 budget from 1545 GMT.
Analysts forecast a one to two percentage point cut in the standard rate of income tax, taking it to 26 percent, as part of an overall package of tax cuts totalling 300 million punts or more.
They also expect Quinn to pencil in an exchange borrowing target of between 600 and 750 million punts for 1997. Last year's EBR was 437 million punts.

"The Irish market has underperformed today. There is a little apprehension about the budget," said Padraig Garvey, economist at Riada. "It's highly unlikely we'll get an EBR number in line with last year."
For the bond market, the EBR is key, dictating as it does the amount of supply that can be expected through government issuance over the next year.
"The budget will be fairly expansionary but we expect an EBR close to 600 (million punts)," the dealer said.
Given that sort of borrowing figure from Quinn, the dealer said the 10-year part of the Irish curve could offer value.
"The short-end is expensive but given a good EBR figure, you could buy the 10-year on the spreads tomorrow," he said.
